education.title: The Small-Cap Discount Anomaly
education.content:
Russell 2000 forward P/E trades at a 31% discount to the S&P 500. That is the widest gap in 25 years.

Historically, discounts above 20% have preceded small-cap outperformance in 8 of 10 instances over the subsequent 18 months. The median excess return: 14.2 percentage points.

The last time the gap exceeded 30% was March 2001. Small caps outperformed large caps by 22% over the following two years. The current gap opened in Q3 2025 and has persisted for nine months.

Our screening system targets sub-$500M companies by design. The structural discount is the tailwind.

Not financial advice.

education.title: Why We Screen 1,279 Stocks to Find Three
education.content:
Most stock pickers start with an idea and look for confirming data. Our system starts with 1,279 stocks and eliminates 99.8% of them.

Last scan: 30 showed momentum inflection. 18 cleared combined filters. Six survived theme quality scoring. Three made it through the forensic audit stage.

The rejection rate is not a bug. A study by Bessembinder (2018) found that just 4% of publicly traded US stocks accounted for the entire net wealth creation in equities since 1926. The other 96% collectively matched Treasury bills.

Finding the 4% requires eliminating the 96%. That is what the filter chain does.

Not financial advice.

education.title: Cash Floor Investing
education.content:
What does it mean when a company's cash exceeds its enterprise value?

It means the market is paying you to take the business. $CYRX has $411M in cash and a market cap near $480M. Enterprise value: $70M. The business generated $192M in revenue last year.

This is a cash floor. If the company shut down tomorrow, liquidated, and returned cash to shareholders, you would receive approximately $8.25 per share. The stock trades at $9.67.

Maximum downside from the cash floor: 15%. Maximum upside if the business reaches profitability and re-rates to 2.5x revenue: 65%.

The asymmetry is the thesis.

Not financial advice.

education.title: The Insider Buying Signal
education.content:
Lakonishok and Lee (2001, Journal of Finance) tracked 10 years of insider transactions across all US public companies. One finding stood out.

When a CEO buys shares on the open market at a company below $500M market cap, the stock outperformed the market by an average of 11.2% over the following 12 months. The signal was strongest when the purchase represented more than 0.5% of the CEO's reported compensation.

$SVCO's CEO Walden Rhines bought $170K of open-market shares at the all-time low. He previously grew Mentor Graphics from $400M revenue to a $4.5B acquisition by Siemens.

Insider purchases are not guarantees. They are information.

Not financial advice.

scanner.title: The Funnel: 1,279 to 3
scanner.content:
Last Friday's screening: 1,279 tickers loaded across all US exchanges.

30 showed momentum inflection. 18 cleared combined filters across 6 distinct themes. Three survived the forensic audit stage.

All three sit within the Biotech Capital Cycle force, targeting different nodes of the pipeline: cold chain logistics, autoimmune cell therapy, and cardiovascular drug development. 100% healthcare concentration, but three distinct sub-themes with uncorrelated catalysts.

99.8% eliminated. One conviction 8. One conviction 7. One conviction 6.

The scanner does not chase narrative. It scores catalyst density, competitive moat, capital structure, and timing.

Not financial advice.

scanner.title: The $91 Stock We Walked Away From
scanner.content:
This month we screened a submarine hardware manufacturer riding a $1.01 trillion defence budget. Monopolistic supplier. Record $515.6M backlog. 2.3x book-to-bill ratio.

The theme scored 8.75 out of 10. Highest in the session.

We walked away.

The stock had tripled from its 52-week low. Trading at $91 against a $73 analyst consensus. 68x trailing P/E versus an 18-22x peer average. The momentum signal was real. The entry was not.

Our system does not chase confirmed winners at full valuation. It finds them before the market does. $GHM goes on the watchlist at $65-70.

Not financial advice.

scanner.title: Conviction Drift: Why We Removed a 47% Grower
scanner.content:
A cross-border payments company processing transactions for six of the Magnificent Seven. Revenue growing 47%. Return on equity 35.6%. Forward P/E of 14.9x against a 39.5x fintech peer average.

The screening system flagged it. The forensic audit passed it. Then the final review removed it.

The reason: conviction drift. Between the initial screen and the final review, the conviction score inflated from a cautious pass to an aggressive buy without any new material finding. The company trades at $3.9 billion market cap, eight times our system's target range. General Atlantic is actively selling. No structural force alignment.

Good numbers are not enough. System fit matters.

Not financial advice.
